Disease Outbreak Disrupts Technology Services Industry in Democratic Republic of the Congo

Kinshasa, June 14 – An outbreak of viral hemorrhagic fever at several Technology Services industry sites in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has led to major workplace disruptions, with multiple firms reporting staff shortages and suspended operations, industry sources said Friday.

According to the Congolese Technology Services Association, at least seven major companies, including Kivu Digital Solutions and CongoTech Partners, have confirmed cases among their employees at offices and data centers in Kinshasa and Lubumbashi. “As of this morning, over 120 workers across our member firms are either hospitalized or in home isolation,” said Jean-Pierre Kasongo, spokesperson for the association.

The outbreak, first detected last week among support staff at a technology park in Lubumbashi, has since been traced to at least four additional sites where close-contact work is common. “We have temporarily closed our Lubumbashi support center and shifted essential operations to remote work, but service delivery is already affected,” said Monique Ilunga, human resources director at CongoTech Partners.

Industry analysts say the outbreak has forced the postponement of several major software rollouts and cloud migration projects, with project teams unable to access secure on-site infrastructure. “We’re seeing a 35-40% workforce reduction in affected firms, which is significant in a sector that relies on specialized talent,” said Aimé Mbuyi, an independent technology consultant.

Unions representing technology workers have called for more robust health measures at industry sites, including expanded testing and on-site medical staff. “Our members are deeply concerned about workplace safety and want clear protocols before returning to affected offices,” said Josephine Mputu, secretary of the National Technology Workers Union.

The Technology Services Association stated it is working with health authorities to trace contacts and contain the outbreak, but warned that further disruptions are likely in the coming weeks.
